summary: Presents operational, policy and security recommendations for operators of DNS recursive resolvers that offer privacy services. It helps operators decide deliberately which services to provide and understand the effects of their choices. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: If you run a service that answers other people's website name lookups, you could see what they look up. This document advises how to run it in a way that respects their privacy.

subtitle: What to do, and what to promise users, when you run a DNS resolver that offers privacy.

tldr.problem: Encrypting DNS on the wire does not stop the resolver operator from seeing every query, so users must trust the operator, who needs guidance on running a privacy service well.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gives threat, optimization and extra-option recommendations for data on the wire, data at rest and data sent onwards, and an outline for a published Recursive operator Privacy Statement (RPS).
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice with three compliance levels, and operators SHOULD publish an RPS so users can compare services.

today: RFC 8932 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 232), published in October 2020, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself says a BCP on privacy and security is a point-in-time statement, so readers should look for updates.

sections.title: Why Operators Need Guidance
sections.content:
Almost every Internet activity starts with a DNS query, yet the DNS was not designed with strong privacy. Newer protocols encrypt DNS messages on the wire, and more people now use "public resolvers" instead of their network's default. Encryption protects against some attacks, but the resolver operator still has, in principle, full visibility of each user's query data and transport identifiers. A trust relationship between user and operator is therefore assumed.

The document has two goals: operational and policy guidance for DNS over encrypted transports and data handling, and a framework for a Recursive operator Privacy Statement (RPS), a document that outlines the operator's practices and commitments. It does not define a particular statement or give legal advice. The authors also note that a BCP on privacy and security is a point-in-time statement, so readers should look for updates.
sections.eli5: Even with a sealed envelope, the post office that opens your mail to deliver it can still read it. So you need to be able to trust the post office, and it should say how it behaves.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
The document covers best practice for recursive resolvers serving clients such as stub resolvers or forwarders. Choices made only by end users, and operators of authoritative nameservers, are out of scope. It looks at three areas: data on the wire between client and server, data at rest on a server (for example in logs), and data sent onwards from the server, either on the wire or shared with a third party.

Areas 2 and 3 could equally apply to operators who offer only unencrypted DNS but want to follow privacy best practice. Much of the threat analysis is taken from RFC 7626 and RFC 6973.
sections.eli5: This guide is for the people who answer lookups, not for the people asking, and it looks at three places a secret could leak.

sections.title: Threats, Actions and Compliance Levels
sections.content:
Each topic first names the threats, from RFC 6973 or specific to DNS privacy services (such as certificate management or availability problems), then lists actions. There are three classes of action: threat mitigation, optimization and additional options.

The document uses no normative words in its recommendations. Instead a service is minimally compliant when it implements all threat mitigations, moderately compliant when it also implements the optimizations, and maximally compliant with the additional options too. Services SHOULD implement these where appropriate, and compliance to the indicated level remains a normative requirement.
sections.eli5: There are three levels, like bronze, silver and gold. The must-do safety steps give you bronze, and more steps get you the higher medals.

sections.title: Protecting Data on the Wire
sections.content:
For transport, a privacy service can offer DNS over TLS (DoT) or DNS over HTTPS (DoH). DNS over DTLS is Experimental with no known implementations at the time of writing. DoT clients using the "Strict Privacy" profile need to authenticate the server, so the service must provide X.509 certificates or SPKI pin sets. Certificate management is called one of the more challenging parts for traditional DNS operators. Operators are told to follow RFC 7525 on revocation, automate certificate issuance and renewal (for example with ACME), monitor expiry and choose a short, memorable authentication domain name.

For DoT, mitigations include implementing only (D)TLS 1.2 or later, EDNS(0) padding, not degrading service for clients that do not use session resumption, and offering DoT on both port 853 and 443. For DoH, clients must be able to forgo HTTP cookies, padding should be used, and clients should not need extra headers.

All DNS privacy services must perform DNSSEC validation and be able to give DNSSEC records to the client, because encryption does not remove the need for DNSSEC. Services should match the availability and the service options (such as filtering) of their unencrypted offering, and operators who lose plaintext monitoring may need resolver-based tools such as dnstap. Fronting DoT with a plain TLS proxy can hide client addresses from the nameserver, which makes ACLs, response rate limiting and DNS64 hard or impossible there.
sections.eli5: Put the question in a sealed envelope, prove who you are with a real ID, keep the shop open as reliably as before, and do not treat private customers worse than others.

sections.title: Data at Rest on the Server
sections.content:
Data retention should be minimized or avoided entirely. If data is kept, it should be encrypted and aggregated, pseudonymized or anonymized where possible. Transient data should be held for the shortest period feasible, logs only as long as needed to run the service and meet regulation, access limited to personnel who need it, and users tracked only to detect and remedy malicious or anomalous use. Full-disk encryption for logs is an optimization.

The document says there is no generally agreed solution or standard for making traffic logs privacy-free. It separates anonymization, where a person is indistinguishable within a set, from pseudonymization, where identity is deterministically replaced and can be reversed if the scheme is known. The client IP address is the major vector for linking queries to an individual, and no single pseudonymization method is widely recognized as suitable for most uses. Other correlation data, such as OS and TLS fingerprints, TCP behavior and client identifiers in EDNS(0) options, should be minimized or discarded. Cache snooping is countered by limiting access and non-recursive queries.
sections.eli5: Do not write down more than you need, throw old notes away, lock up the notes you keep, and cover up names so nobody can tell whose question was whose.

sections.title: Data Sent Onwards
sections.content:
The server should implement QNAME minimization and honor a SOURCE PREFIX-LENGTH of 0 in an EDNS(0) Client Subnet (ECS) option. As an optimization it should either not send ECS upstream at all or offer one service that sends it and one that does not. Operators that do send ECS should use the shortest prefix that is operationally feasible, ideally allowlist the upstream servers, and state in policy the prefix length and policy used.

Additional options include aggressive use of the DNSSEC-validated cache, RFC 8020 behavior and running a local copy of the root zone. Because upstream queries are cleartext at the time of writing, small resolvers risk exposing their users and ought to mix in generated traffic, though no standardized technique exists. Small operators might forward local traffic over an encrypted protocol to a larger resolver with an aligned privacy policy.

Operators should not share identifiable data with third parties. If they do in specific circumstances, they should publish the terms, and they should consider guidelines for sharing aggregated or anonymized data for research.
sections.eli5: When your resolver asks other servers for help, it should tell them as little about you as possible, and it should never hand your details to strangers.

sections.title: The Recursive Operator Privacy Statement
sections.content:
To comply with this BCP, a recursive operator SHOULD publish an RPS. Using the given outline and its headings in order helps people compare operators. Apart from the order of headings, the content of the outline is non-normative, covers only the technical operation of the service and is not a basis for legal documents.

The Policy part covers the treatment of IP addresses as personal data, data collection and sharing, exceptions, associated entities, correlation and result filtering (security, mandatory legal, voluntary legal and other reasons). The Practice part covers deviations, client-facing capabilities, upstream capabilities, support and data processing. For accountability, transparency reports may build trust, independent monitoring could check ECS, QNAME minimization, padding, filtering and uptime, and operators could engage a third-party auditor.
sections.eli5: Write a clear page saying what you do with people's questions and what you promise, in the same order everyone else uses, so people can compare.

sections.title: Security Considerations and IANA
sections.content:
The document has no IANA actions. Its security section points elsewhere: security considerations for DNS over TCP are in RFC 7766, for DoT in RFC 7858 and RFC 8310, for DoH in RFC 8484, and for DNSSEC in RFC 4033, RFC 4034 and RFC 4035.

The main security guidance is in the recommendations themselves, such as server authentication, DNSSEC validation and protecting service availability against denial-of-service attacks.
sections.eli5: For the deep details of each lock, this guide points you to the documents that describe each one.
